newsitem.title: USA: Residents of Simpson's old haunt shrug shoulders.
newsitem.headline: Residents of Simpson's old haunt shrug shoulders.

text.p: A jury verdict blaming O.J. Simpson for the killings of his ex-wife and her friend drew a muted response on Tuesday in the neighbourhood where he grew up.
Some residents said only money was at stake in the civil trial.

Except for cars screeching around the block, the area of drab housing projects in the Potrero Hill district of San Francisco where Simpson spent his youth was quiet after the civil trial jury in Santa Monica announced its verdict.
The low-key reaction was in sharp contrast to the jubilation in the area when Simpson, a local hero, was acquitted of double-murder charges in his criminal trial in October 1995.

On Tuesday, a civil trial jury found the former football star responsible for a deadly 1994 knife attack on his ex-wife Nicole Brown Simpson and her friend Ronald Goldman and ordered him to pay $8.5 million in compensatory damages.
While some Potrero Hill residents expressed surprise at the size of the damages, others shrugged their shoulders.

"It's really no big deal. They had to get him somehow," one young man, who declined to give his name, said. "He'll figure out how to pay them and still have money," he said, saying Simpson might make a movie or write a book to raise the cash.

Many residents of the largely-black area strongly supported Simpson during the criminal trial and asserted his innocence. But perhaps because the Simpson saga has gone on for so long, passions have died down. Most residents interviewed said they paid much less attention to the civil trial than they did to the criminal case.
"Today it's like no big deal. They are fighting just for money now," said Marcelino Padilla, 31, who was repairing his car outside a Potrero Hill store.
At stake in the criminal trial, by contrast, was whether or not Simpson would spend the rest of his life in prison.
But several residents said it seemed to them like double jeopardy that Simpson was found responsible for the attack in a civil trial after being acquitted in the criminal trial.

"I really don't understand because I feel like if you've got acquitted on one trial, there shouldn't be no other one," Red Johnson, 24, said as he left the Potrero Hill Recreation Centre, where Simpson played sports as a youth.
A mural painted on the wall of the centre shows Simpson in a Buffalo Bills uniform with his number 32 on it.
"I believe he's innocent. I feel it's wrong that they try to say that he did it," added Johnson, a football player who said Simpson was his hero.
Simpson's parents divorced when he was five and his mother Eunice raised Simpson, his brother and two sisters in a two-bedroom unit in the tough Potrero Hill projects.

Simpson, now 49, spent his teenage years as a gang leader there, fighting in the streets and engaging in petty crime. He went on to fame and fortune as a sports star, actor and television personality.
Charlie Bryant, 37, a director at the recreation centre who was watching youths play basketball inside, said the case was "between Simpson and the white community."
"Hopefully everybody got what they wanted," he said. Bryant, who used to know Simpson, said it seemed unfair that Simpson should have faced a second, civil, trial.
"But then again you've got to look at O.J. That's the life he wanted to live," he added.
